stages.name: Evaluating monetary policy and its risks
stages.title: Evaluating monetary policy and its risks
stages.sub: The student can evaluate interest rate and money supply changes, and explain why monetary policy is hard to get right in practice.

steps.q: A central bank cuts interest rates to boost spending. But some households have savings, not loans, and now earn less interest. Will the cut help every household equally?
steps.right: No, the effect depends on each household's situation
steps.wrong: Yes, lower rates help every household the same way
steps.hint: Think about a saver versus a borrower with a mortgage.

steps.q: The economy has already slowed for two months before the data confirms it. What has happened to the central bank's ability to act on time?
steps.right: It has already lost time before it even knows there is a problem
steps.wrong: It has lost no time, since it can act the moment the slowdown starts
steps.hint: Data takes time to collect and confirm - during that time, does the bank know what is happening?

steps.q: The central bank cuts rates today. Will households and firms change their borrowing and spending decisions immediately, or only after months of adjusting contracts, mortgages and plans?
steps.right: Only after a delay, as decisions adjust over time
steps.wrong: Immediately, as soon as the rate changes
steps.hint: Think about someone on a fixed-rate mortgage, or a firm partway through a project.
steps.pre: That delay before the change actually affects the economy is an

steps.q: A central bank sets policy based on next year's predicted growth and inflation. If that prediction turns out to be wrong, was the policy based on reliable information?
steps.right: No, it was based on a mistaken prediction
steps.wrong: Yes, predictions are treated as certain facts
steps.hint: Policy is set now, but the numbers it relies on are guesses about the future.

steps.q: Given that policymakers cannot spot problems instantly, cannot see effects appear immediately, and cannot predict the future perfectly, can they ever be fully confident a policy will work as planned?
steps.right: No, there is always a risk it will not work as expected
steps.wrong: Yes, once the mechanism is understood, the outcome is certain
steps.hint: Combine the delays in spotting and reacting with the chance the forecast itself is wrong.
